seo.title: HTS Chapter 30: Pharmaceutical Products — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Complete searchable duty table for all 198 HTS Chapter 30 tariff lines — vaccines, antibodies, blood products, medicines, bandages and other pharmaceutical goods. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, filterable by product name.

overview.intro:
Chapter 30 covers finished pharmaceuticals — vaccines, antibodies and blood products (3002), medicines in bulk (3003) and in doses or retail packs (3004), bandages and dressings (3005) and other pharmaceutical goods such as surgical sutures, contraceptives and ostomy appliances (3006). It is one of the largest chapters by value: the U.S. imported **$213.8B** of these goods in 2025, a fifth of it from Ireland.

The printed rate is almost always **Free**: 192 of the **198 tariff lines** carry no duty, and the six that do are niche 3006 products. What decides the cost is the extra duty on top. Since September 29, 2026, **patented drugs** on a list of 77 lines pay a Section 232 duty of **100%**, cut to **15%** for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland and to **0%** for the UK; **generic drugs pay nothing extra**. Dressings and a few 3006 lines also pay a 10–12.5% Section 301 duty for 60 economies (see Rates by country). And for any shipment, FDA approval and registration decide whether the product can be sold at all.

productGroups.label: Glands, organs & heparin
productGroups.blurb: Dried glands and organ extracts used in organotherapy, plus heparin and its salts and other human or animal substances prepared for treatment. Every line is Free.

productGroups.label: Blood, antisera, vaccines & immunological products
productGroups.blurb: The biologics heading. It covers monoclonal antibodies and other immunological products, plasma and blood fractions, vaccines, and cell therapy products. It is the largest group by value, and every line is Free.

productGroups.label: Medicaments, not in measured doses (bulk)
productGroups.blurb: Mixed medicines shipped in bulk, not yet in doses or retail packs, for finishing or packaging in the U.S.: antibiotics, insulin, hormones, alkaloids and anti-infectives. Every line is Free.

productGroups.label: Medicaments in measured doses or retail packs
productGroups.blurb: Finished medicines in doses or retail packs: tablets, capsules, injections, pens and creams, split by active ingredient and therapy area. It has the most lines in the chapter (138), and every one is Free.

productGroups.label: Bandages, gauze & dressings
productGroups.blurb: Wadding, gauze, bandages, adhesive dressings and laparotomy sponges, whether or not coated with medicine, put up for retail or medical use. Every line is Free.

productGroups.label: Other pharmaceutical goods (Note 4)
productGroups.blurb: Only the goods listed in Chapter 30 Note 4: sutures, X-ray contrast and diagnostic reagents, dental cements, first-aid kits, contraceptives, ostomy appliances and clinical-trial placebos. This is the only heading with duty. Six lines are dutiable: medical lubricating gels (5%), ostomy appliances (4.2%) and four kinds of placebo (sugar-based, starch-based, liquid and other); the rest are Free.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: A patented antibody from Ireland
workedExamples.body: The base rate is Free. As a patented drug on the Section 232 list from the EU, it pays **15% of its value in place of the base rate** (9903.04.62): a $10M shipment owes **$1.5M**. If the maker has an onshoring and pricing agreement with the U.S. government, the rate is **0%** (9903.04.65).

workedExamples.title: Generic tablets from India
workedExamples.body: The base rate is Free and generics are excluded from the Section 232 duty (9903.04.67), so a $2M container of generic tablets owes **$0** in duty. Most medicines are also exempt from the Section 301 tariffs. The same tablets sold as a patented brand would pay **100%**, because India has no reduced rate.

workedExamples.title: Ostomy pouches from China
workedExamples.body: One of the few dutiable lines: **4.2%** base rate. China is one of the 60 Section 301 economies, so a further **12.5%** applies (9903.05.31): **16.7%** in total, or **$16,700** on a $100,000 shipment. The same pouches from Singapore are Free under the Singapore FTA but still pay the 12.5% Section 301 duty.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) Foods or beverages (such as dietetic, diabetic or fortified foods, food supplements, tonic beverages and mineral waters), other than nutritional preparations for intravenous administration (section IV); (b) Products, such as tablets, chewing gum or patches (transdermal systems), containing nicotine and intended to assist tobacco use cessation (heading 2404); (c) Plasters specially calcined or finely ground for use in dentistry (heading 2520); (d) Aqueous distillates or aqueous solutions of essential oils, suitable for medicinal uses (heading 3301); (e) Preparations of headings 3303 to 3307, even if they have therapeutic or prophylactic properties; (f) Soap or other products of heading 3401 containing added medicaments; (g) Preparations with a basis of plaster for use in dentistry (heading 3407); (h) Blood albumin not prepared for therapeutic or prophylactic uses (heading 3502); or (ij) Diagnostic reagents of heading 3822.

**Note 2.** For the purposes of heading 3002, the expression "immunological products" applies to peptides and proteins (other than goods of heading 2937) which are directly involved in the regulation of immunological processes, such as monoclonal antibodies (MAB), antibody fragments, antibody conjugates and antibody fragment conjugates, interleukins, interferons (IFN), chemokines and certain tumor necrosis factors (TNF), growth factors (GF), hematopoietins and colony stimulating factors (CSF).

**Note 3.** For the purposes of headings 3003 and 3004 and of note 4(d) to this chapter the following are to be treated-- (a) As unmixed products: (1) Unmixed products dissolved in water; (2) All goods of chapter 28 or 29; and (3) Simple vegetable extracts of heading 1302, merely standardized or dissolved in any solvent; (b) As products which have been mixed: (1) Colloidal solutions and suspensions (other than colloidal sulfur); (2) Vegetable extracts obtained by the treatment of mixtures of vegetable materials; and (3) Salts and concentrates obtained by evaporating natural mineral waters.

**Note 4.** Heading 3006 applies only to the following, which are to be classified in that heading and in no other heading of the tariff schedule: (a) Sterile surgical catgut, similar sterile suture materials (including sterile absorbable surgical or dental yarns) and sterile tissue adhesives for surgical wound closure; (b) Sterile laminaria and sterile laminaria tents; (c) Sterile absorbable surgical or dental hemostatics, sterile surgical or dental adhesion barriers, whether or not absorbable; (d) Opacifying preparations for X-ray examinations and diagnostic reagents designed to be administered to the patient, being unmixed products put up in measured doses or products consisting of two or more ingredients which have been mixed together for such uses; (e) Placebos and blinded (or double-blinded) clinical trial kits for use in recognized clinical trials, put up in measured doses, even if they might contain active medicaments. (f) Dental cements and other dental fillings; bone reconstruction cements; (g) First-aid boxes and kits; (h) Chemical contraceptive preparations based on hormones, on other products of heading 2937 or on spermicides; (ij) Gel preparations designed to be used in human or veterinary medicine as a lubricant for parts of the body for surgical operations or physical examinations or as a coupling agent between the body and medical instruments; (k) Waste pharmaceuticals, that is, pharmaceutical products which are unfit for their original intended purpose, for example, because of expiry of shelf life; and (l) Appliances identifiable for ostomy use, that is, colostomy, ileostomy and urostomy pouches cut to shape and their adhesive wafers or faceplates.

**Subheading Note 1.** For the purposes of subheadings 3002.13 and 3002.14, the following are to be treated: (a) As unmixed products, pure products, whether or not containing impurities; (b) As products which have been mixed: (1) The products mentioned in (a) above dissolved in water or in other solvents; (2) The products mentioned in (a) and (b)(1) above with an added stabilizer necessary for their preservation or transport; and (3) The products mentioned in (a), (b)(1) and (b)(2) above with any other additive.

**Subheading Note 2.** Subheadings 3003.60 and 3004.60 cover medicaments containing artemisinin (INN) for oral ingestion combined with other pharmaceutical active ingredients, or containing any of the following active principles, whether or not combined with other pharmaceutical active ingredients: amodiaquine (INN); artelinic acid or its salts; artenimol (INN); artemotil (INN); artemether (INN); artesunate (INN); chloroquine (INN); dihydroartemisinin (INN); lumafantrine (INN); mefloquine (INN); piperaquine (INN); pyrimethamine (INN) or sulfadoxine (INN).

effectiveDuty.note: Chapter-level duty paid in 2024 from tariff_trade_analytics (as cited in issue #1770): about $5.2M on $168.9B of customs value. Per-country and per-line duty come from the same table in production.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. pharmaceutical imports were **$213.82B in 2025**, flat on 2024 (+0.5%). Two lines make up three-quarters of the total. **3004.90** ($82.51B) is finished medicines in doses or retail packs, ready for patients. **3002.15** ($78.73B) is "immunological products" in doses: monoclonal antibodies, interferons and similar proteins (Note 2), which covers much of today's biologic drugs.

**Why these countries.** Ireland (19.9%), Germany, Switzerland, Belgium and Singapore host large drug-substance and fill-finish plants run by U.S. and European drugmakers. Ireland has drawn 17 of the top 20 drugmakers, helped by its long-standing 12.5% corporate tax rate. Eli Lilly makes Zepbound in Cork. India (7.1%) is different: it ships mostly generic tablets under 3004.

**2023 → 2024 (+20%).** Imports rose $34.8B. Ireland alone added $14.3B, a rise Irish reporting ties in large part to Lilly's GLP-1 drug Zepbound.

**2025: a spike, then a hangover.** After the U.S. opened a Section 232 investigation into pharmaceuticals, companies brought shipments forward. U.S. imports from Ireland reached nearly $31B in March 2025 alone. Ireland's CSO then reported steep falls through December as U.S. inventories were worked down. The spike and the drawdown roughly cancelled out, leaving Ireland down 15% and the total flat. Singapore's pharma shipments to the U.S. fell 93.5% in July 2025 alone, and Singapore ended the year down 28%. Germany (+52%) and France (+185%) gained share. Germany's own data show its pharma exports to the U.S. barely rose, so origin recording may explain part of that gap. We found no reporting that explains France's jump.

The 6 dutiable lines are all in 3006, so duty paid stays near zero. The Section 232 tariffs on patented drugs, signed April 2, 2026, are covered under Tariff updates.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 30: Pharmaceutical Products — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 30 Pharmaceutical Tariff Updates — Section 232 Drug Tariffs Since 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 30 (pharmaceutical products) since January 2025: the Section 232 100% duty on patented drugs (15% EU/Japan/Korea/Switzerland, 0% UK, generics exempt), the end of IEEPA tariffs, Section 301, and all 198 lines.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares the **2025 Basic Edition** of the tariff schedule, in force at the start of 2025, with the current **2026 Revision 20**. No Chapter 30 base rate changed: 192 of the 198 lines are still Free and the six dutiable lines in heading 3006 carry the same rates as before.

What changed is the extra duty on top. Since **September 29, 2026** (July 31 for 17 large drugmakers), patented (brand-name) medicines on a list of 77 Chapter 30 lines pay a **Section 232 duty of 100%**, cut to **15%** for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland and to **0%** for the UK. **Generic drugs pay nothing extra.** The IEEPA tariffs of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. The Section 301 tariffs in force since July 24, 2026 exempt almost all of Chapter 30; they reach only bandages and dressings (3005) and four 3006 subheadings (9 lines).

The line list grew from 144 to 198. **102 lines are new**: 68 numbers that did not exist in 2025 and 34 numbers in 3004.90.92 that were reused for a different drug. They came in two statistical updates, Revision 2 (in force January 30, 2026) and Revision 11 (in force July 1, 2026). They split "Other" baskets into named, mostly generic hospital drugs (ceftriaxone, vancomycin, heparin, insulin glargine, propofol and others). The schedule does not say why; the likely aim is to track imports of individual essential drugs, but we have not found an official statement. 14 old "Other" lines were retired.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 30 from any country: the Section 232 pharmaceutical duty (default, deal and UK rates), the 2026 Section 301 tariffs and the older China Section 301 lists. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: Covers only patented drugs (Orange Book or Purple Book, valid U.S. patent) and their ingredients on the U.S. note 40(c) list: 77 lines in 3002, 3003 and 3004. Generics and biosimilars: no extra duty (9903.04.67). Other ways to pay less: company onshoring plan 20% (9903.04.64; no company eligible as of CBP's July 30, 2026 guidance); onshoring plus an MFN drug-pricing agreement with HHS 0% until January 20, 2029 (9903.04.65); orphan drugs, plasma-derived therapies, cell and gene therapies, ADCs, fertility and nuclear medicines from listed countries 0% (9903.04.66); U.S.-made API put into dosage form abroad (9903.04.68); clinical trials and R&D (9903.04.70). Annex III companies have paid since July 31, 2026; everyone else since September 29, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A patented cancer biologic from Singapore (3002.15) with no company agreement pays 100% of its value; a generic from the same plant pays nothing extra. The 100% is the total, not 100% on top of the base rate, and every listed line is Free anyway.

inEffect.country: EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Liechtenstein
inEffect.measure: Section 232 duty on patented pharmaceuticals (deal rate)
inEffect.exemption: Same scope as 9903.04.60: patented drugs only. Generics: no extra duty (9903.04.67). The lower company and specialty headings (9903.04.65, 9903.04.66, 9903.04.70) apply when they give a lower rate; all five are on the 9903.04.66 country list.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A patented antibody from Ireland or Germany (3002.15) pays 15% of its value in total. If the company has both an onshoring plan and an MFN pricing agreement, it pays 0%.

inEffect.measure: Section 232 duty on patented pharmaceuticals (UK rate)
inEffect.exemption: Set at +10% by Proclamation 11020, then cut to +0% from July 31, 2026 under the U.S.–UK pharmaceutical pricing arrangement. Patented UK drugs must still be entered under 9903.04.63.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A patented medicine made in the UK pays only its base rate, which is Free for every listed line.

inEffect.country: 60 economies (incl. EU, Switzerland, Japan, India, Singapore, China, UK)
inEffect.exemption: Most of Chapter 30 is exempt: 45 subheadings are on the U.S. note 52(b) list (9903.05.86) and 7 more are exempt when for pharmaceutical use (9903.05.89). Patented drugs under 9903.04.60–9903.04.66 are also excluded (9903.05.90). What is left: all of 3005 (bandages, gauze, dressings) and 3006.10.01, 3006.40.00, 3006.50.00 and 3006.91.00 (9 lines). EU goods pay 10% in place of the base rate (9903.05.39); Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5% in place of the base rate; India, UK, Canada and Mexico +10%; China, Singapore and most others +12.5%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).
inEffect.whatItMeans: Sterile gauze from China (3005.90) pays 12.5%; an ostomy pouch from Germany (3006.91, base 4.2%) pays 10% in total. Vaccines, insulin and tablets pay none of this.

inEffect.exemption: Not new: in force before 2025 and unchanged since. List 3 (+25%, 9903.88.03) covers 3006.93.60 and 3006.93.80; List 4A (+7.5%, 9903.88.15) covers 3006.93.20 and 3006.93.50. No other Chapter 30 subheading is on a China Section 301 list.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Chinese placebos or clinical trial kits (3006.93.80, base 5%) pay 30%; other Chinese Chapter 30 goods are untouched by these lists.

changes.title: No Chapter 30 base-rate changes
changes.detail: Every line that exists in both editions carries the same General rate in the 2026 Revision 20 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. The six dutiable lines (3006.70, 3006.91, 3006.93.20, 3006.93.50, 3006.93.60, 3006.93.80) are unchanged; everything else is Free.

changes.title: Section 232 pharmaceutical duty extended to all companies
changes.detail: The interim 0% heading for companies not named in Annex III (9903.04.61) ended at 12:01 a.m. ET. Patented drugs from every company now pay 100% (9903.04.60) unless a lower heading applies. CBP's updated guidance is CSMS # 70054007 (September 28, 2026); we could not open the CBP copy and relied on the HTS text for the rates.

changes.title: Specialty-drug 0% rate defined; 3002.13–3002.15 and 3004.49 taken off the zero list
changes.detail: Commerce named the countries whose orphan drugs, plasma-derived therapies, cell and gene therapies, ADCs and similar products get 0% under 9903.04.66, including the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, the UK and India (Singapore and China are not on the list). It also removed 3002.13.00, 3002.14.00, 3002.15.00 and 3004.49.00 from Annex IV, the list of codes held at zero, so patented antibodies and other immunological products in those codes now pay the Section 232 rate. CBP added 9903.04.70 (0%) for clinical-trial and R&D use from September 29.

changes.title: UK rate on patented drugs cut to zero
changes.detail: Commerce found the U.S.–UK pharmaceutical pricing arrangement conditions met and changed 9903.04.63 from +10% to +0%.

changes.title: Section 232 pharmaceutical duty starts for the 17 Annex III companies
changes.detail: Patented drugs and their ingredients on the U.S. note 40(c) list (77 Chapter 30 lines plus Chapter 29 APIs) imported for the large drugmakers named in Annex III pay 100%, 15% for EU/Japan/Korea/Swiss origin, 0% if the company has onshoring and MFN pricing agreements (Annex II). Generics pay nothing extra (9903.04.67). We have not been able to read the Annex III company names.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies; most of Chapter 30 exempt
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). Only 3005 and 3006.10.01, 3006.40.00, 3006.50.00 and 3006.91.00 (9 lines) are not exempted by U.S. note 52(b) or 52(e).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: 36 statistical lines added or renumbered (Revision 11)
changes.detail: 3004.90.92 was renumbered again to make room for named drugs such as hydroxyurea, tacrolimus, enoxaparin, midazolam, propofol and ondansetron. Rates did not change; all are Free.

changes.title: Section 232 duties on patented pharmaceuticals proclaimed
changes.detail: Proclamation 11020 set 100% on patented drugs and ingredients, 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 10% for the UK, 20% with an approved onshoring plan (rising to 100% on April 2, 2030) and 0% with onshoring plus MFN pricing agreements. Generics, biosimilars and purchases for the Strategic API Reserve are excluded.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces IEEPA tariffs; most of Chapter 30 exempt
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01), with the same product exemption list the reciprocal tariff used: 47 of the 60 Chapter 30 subheadings were exempt (9903.03.03). The 13 others (3003.31, 3003.43, 3003.60, 3004.43, all of 3005, 3006.10.01, 3006.40, 3006.50, 3006.91, 3006.92) paid +10%.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended every IEEPA duty and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 20 but are shaded as expired.

changes.title: 66 statistical lines added or renumbered (Revision 2)
changes.detail: Heparin was split out of 3001.90.01, and 3004 baskets were split into named drugs such as ceftriaxone, vancomycin, meropenem, insulin glargine, dexamethasone, epinephrine and levothyroxine. Rates did not change.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 100% tariff on branded drugs announced for October 1, 2025, not implemented
changes.detail: The President announced on social media a 100% tariff on branded or patented drugs from October 1, 2025, unless the company was building a U.S. plant. No proclamation followed in 2025 and nothing was collected; the duty arrived with Proclamation 11020 in April 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 investigation of pharmaceuticals opened
changes.detail: Commerce began the investigation on April 1, 2025 and asked for comments; the report went to the President on January 5, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff; pharmaceuticals exempt
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx). 47 of the 60 Chapter 30 subheadings were on the Annex II exemption list (9903.01.32); the 13 others, mainly dressings and some 3006 goods, paid the reciprocal rate. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%, with no pharmaceutical exemption
changes.detail: Unlike the reciprocal tariff, the China IEEPA duty (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) applied to all Chapter 30 goods from China and Hong Kong, generics included. +10% from February 4, 2025, +20% from March 4, 2025.

industryAreas.h1: HTS Chapter 30: Pharmaceutical Products — Tariff Rates by Country

seo.title: HTS Chapter 30 Pharmaceutical Tariff Rates by Country — Ireland, Germany, Switzerland, India | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on medicines, vaccines and dressings by country and product group: 100% on patented drugs, 15% for the EU, Japan and Switzerland, 0% for the UK and for generics, plus Section 301 on dressings.
keywords: HTS Chapter 30 tariff rates by country

industryAreas.intro:
For medicines, the total rate depends less on the country than on **whether the drug is patented**. Every line in 3001–3005 and almost all of 3006 is Free, so the only money at stake is the extra duty. Since September 29, 2026, patented drugs on the Section 232 list (77 lines in 3002, 3003 and 3004) pay **100%**, or **15%** from the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland, and **0%** from the UK. **Generics and biosimilars pay nothing extra** from anywhere.

That is why each biologics and dosed-medicine cell below shows two numbers: Free for generics and the patented rate. Companies with onshoring and MFN drug-pricing agreements, and orphan, plasma, cell and gene therapies from listed countries, pay 0% even when patented. The 2026 Section 301 tariffs exempt nearly all of Chapter 30; they reach only bandages and dressings (3005) and a few 3006 goods such as sutures, dental cements, first-aid kits and ostomy appliances.

assumptions: "Free · 15% if patented" means the group mixes lines on the Section 232 list with lines that are not. On listed lines, patented drugs pay the second rate and generics pay nothing; select a cell to see which lines are listed.
Patent status is per product, not per HTS line: a line holds both brand and generic drugs. The schedule cannot tell you how much of a cell is patented, so no blended rate is shown.
The 232 rates of 100% and 15% are totals that replace the base rate (U.S. note 40(d) and (f)). Every listed Chapter 30 line is Free, so the total equals the stated rate.

Company-specific relief is not applied: 0% for companies with onshoring and MFN pricing agreements (9903.04.65, Annex II), 20% with an approved onshoring plan (9903.04.64), and 0% for specialty drugs such as orphan, plasma-derived, cell and gene therapies from listed countries (9903.04.66). Many of the largest drugmakers have such agreements, so actual duty paid on patented drugs is likely well below the headline rate.

Seven subheadings (3003.31, 3003.43, 3003.60, 3004.43, 3006.70, 3006.92, 3006.93.80) are exempt from Section 301 only when "for use in pharmaceutical applications" (9903.05.89). The table assumes that condition is met.
EU goods pay the Section 301 rate as 10% in place of the base rate (9903.05.39), and Japan and Switzerland as 12.5% in place of the base rate; for other countries it is added to the base rate.

Preferences applied: Singapore FTA (SG) and U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement (JP) where the schedule lists them. GSP (A, A+) and the WTO Pharmaceutical Appendix (K) are not applied; K requires the product to be listed in the Pharmaceutical Appendix. The Section 232 duty is charged even when a preference makes the base rate Free (U.S. note 40(b)).
Per-unit rates (40¢/kg + 10.4%, 0.2¢/liter) cannot be added into one percentage without the shipment's weight and volume, so they are shown as written.
"Any other country" shows a range for dressings because only the 60 economies named in the Section 301 action pay it; Canada and Mexico pay nothing on USMCA-qualifying goods.
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 40 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 20. Note 40(c) lists 77 Chapter 30 statistical lines (in 3002, 3003 and 3004) that carry the Section 232 duty; none in 3001, 3005 or 3006. Note 52(b) (9903.05.86) exempts 45 of the 60 Chapter 30 subheadings from Section 301 and note 52(e) (9903.05.89) 7 more for pharmaceutical use; 3005 and 3006.10.01, 3006.40.00, 3006.50.00 and 3006.91.00 are on neither list. The country exception lists in note 52(j) contain no Chapter 30 code. In note 20, only 3006.93.20, 3006.93.50 (List 4A) and 3006.93.60, 3006.93.80 (List 3) are on a China Section 301 list.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 30: Pharmaceutical Products — Import Requirements & Duty-Saving Rules

seo.title: Importing Pharmaceuticals: FDA, DEA & Section 232 Rules and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 30) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The FDA, DEA and USDA requirements for each HTS Chapter 30 line, and the legal ways to pay less: Section 232 generic and country rates, the Section 301 pharma exemption, FTAs, drawback and FTZs.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For medicines the tariff schedule is the easy part: **192 of the chapter's 198 lines are Free**, and the six that are not are all in heading 3006. **What decides whether the goods land is FDA** — every shipment is checked against the maker's registration, the product's listing and its approval or license, and DEA, USDA, CDC or EPA step in for specific products.

The money is now in two newer layers. **Section 232** puts up to 100% on patented drugs on 77 lines in 3002–3004 from September 29, 2026 — with generics, biosimilars, EU/Japanese/Korean/Swiss goods (15% all-in), UK goods and specialty products carved out. **Section 301 forced-labor duties** (10–12.5%) exempt most medicines but reach dressings, sutures, dental cements, first-aid kits and ostomy appliances. Each way to pay less below depends on a document, listed with the rule that creates it.

levers.title: Enter generics and biosimilars under the Section 232 generic heading
levers.saves: The whole Section 232 duty — up to 100% of value — on a drug that would otherwise be treated as patented
levers.appliesTo: 77 lines in 3002–3004 named in U.S. note 40(c): FDA-approved generics (ANDA, therapeutically equivalent 505(b)(2)), biosimilars (351(k)), authorized generics imported by a generic maker, unpatented animal-health products, and their ingredients — heading 9903.04.67
levers.document: The FDA application number (ANDA, 505(b)(2) or 351(k)) for the product, and evidence that no valid U.S. patent or exclusivity covers it (Orange Book / Purple Book status).
levers.caveat: The proclamation exempts generics only "at this time"; Commerce must report within a year whether to cover them. A product listed in the Orange or Purple Book with an unexpired patent is "patented" even if a generic version exists.

levers.title: Use the country rate: EU, Japan, Korea, Switzerland/Liechtenstein capped at 15%; UK at 0%; U.S.-origin API exempt
levers.saves: 85 points on a patented drug from the EU, Japan, Korea or Switzerland (15% all-in instead of 100%); the full 100% on UK-origin goods; the full duty on a dosage form made from U.S.-origin API
levers.appliesTo: The 77 Section 232 lines — headings 9903.04.62 (15% all-in), 9903.04.63 (UK, +0%) and 9903.04.68 (U.S. API packaged in dosage form)
levers.document: Country-of-origin evidence for the finished product (where it was last substantially transformed — for most drugs, where the API was made or the dosage form produced, decided case by case), or proof the API is a product of the United States.
levers.caveat: Origin is not where the goods ship from: an Irish-packed tablet made from Indian API may not be an EU product. The proclamation set the UK at 10%; the current schedule shows +0% — check CBP guidance for the date that applies to your entry. Commerce can raise country rates if a partner misses its commitments.

levers.title: Buy from a company with a Commerce onshoring plan or an MFN pricing agreement
levers.saves: Onshoring plan + MFN pricing agreement: 0% instead of 100% (until January 20, 2029). Onshoring plan alone: 20% instead of 100% (rising to 100% on April 2, 2030)
levers.appliesTo: Patented products on the 77 Section 232 lines, imported for a company Commerce has notified to CBP — headings 9903.04.65 and 9903.04.64
levers.document: Confirmation that the manufacturer is on Commerce's list sent to CBP, plus any information CBP requires at entry.
levers.caveat: The importer cannot apply — the manufacturer's agreement decides it. Industry summaries of CBP guidance report that no company yet qualifies for the 20% onshoring-only rate (unverified). Commerce can re-impose duties retroactively if a company breaks its commitments.

levers.title: Check the specialty-product zero rate (orphan drugs, plasma-derived, cell & gene therapies, ADCs, nuclear medicine, fertility, countermeasures, animal health)
levers.saves: The whole Section 232 duty (0% instead of up to 100%)
levers.appliesTo: Products on the 77 Section 232 lines in the listed categories that Commerce designates by Federal Register notice — heading 9903.04.66. Relevant here: plasma fractions (3002.12), monoclonal-antibody and ADC products (3002.13–3002.15), cell therapies (3002.51), veterinary lines
levers.document: The Commerce Federal Register designation covering the product (and, for orphan drugs, FDA orphan designation for every approved indication).
levers.caveat: Not automatic: the zero rate applies only once Commerce designates the product and finds the source country has a trade-and-security framework or the product meets an urgent U.S. health need. A drug with any non-orphan indication does not qualify as orphan.

levers.title: Enter clinical-trial and R&D material under the non-commercial heading
levers.saves: The whole Section 232 duty on trial supplies of a patented drug
levers.appliesTo: Products on the 77 Section 232 lines solely for clinical trials, research and development or other non-commercial use — heading 9903.04.70
levers.document: Evidence of the non-commercial use: the IND or trial protocol, and consignment to the sponsor or investigator.
levers.caveat: The same goods sold commercially later lose the basis for the claim. Placebos and blinded trial kits are classified separately in 3006.93 and are outside the Section 232 list.

levers.title: Report the pharmaceutical exemption from the Section 301 forced-labor duties
levers.saves: 10% or 12.5% of value, depending on the country (applies to imports from 60 economies including China, India, the EU, Switzerland, Singapore, Japan, Korea and the UK since July 24, 2026)
levers.appliesTo: Almost every line in 3001–3004 and most of 3006 — via heading 9903.05.86 (provisions listed in U.S. note 52(b)) or 9903.05.89 (provisions in U.S. note 52(e), for goods used in pharmaceutical applications)
levers.document: The correct 10-digit classification and the exemption heading on the entry; for 9903.05.89, support that the goods are for pharmaceutical use.
levers.caveat: Not covered by either list: 3005 dressings and bandages, 3006.10 sutures, 3006.40 dental cements, 3006.50 first-aid kits and 3006.91 ostomy appliances — those pay the duty unless another exemption applies.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on Canadian or Mexican dressings, sutures, kits and ostomy appliances
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian or Mexican goods, plus the base rate on ostomy appliances (4.2%)
levers.appliesTo: The lines outside the Section 301 pharmaceutical exemption: 3005 (5 lines), 3006.10, 3006.40, 3006.50, 3006.91 — headings 9903.05.93 (Canada) and 9903.05.94 (Mexico)
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer; the goods must actually be entered free of duty under USMCA.
levers.caveat: Only goods that meet the USMCA rule of origin qualify; Canadian or Mexican assembly from Asian gauze may not.

levers.title: Claim a free trade agreement on the six dutiable 3006 lines
levers.saves: The base rate: 3006.70 gels 5% · 3006.91 ostomy appliances 4.2% · 3006.93.20 sugar placebos 40¢/kg + 10.4% · 3006.93.50 starch placebos 6.4% · 3006.93.60 liquid placebos 0.2¢/liter · 3006.93.80 other placebos 5%
levers.appliesTo: 3006.70, 3006.91, 3006.93.20, 3006.93.50, 3006.93.60, 3006.93.80 — goods originating in an FTA partner shown in the Special column (Australia, Bahrain, Chile, Colombia, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Morocco, Oman, Panama, Peru, Singapore, USMCA, CAFTA-DR; 3006.93.20 via Chapter 98/99 provisions for some partners)
levers.document: The origin certification or declaration the agreement requires, and records showing the product meets its rule of origin.
levers.caveat: An FTA claim removes the base rate only: Section 232 duties apply on top of any FTA rate, and the Section 301 duties apply to FTA-eligible goods except USMCA goods from Canada or Mexico. GSP (A, A+) lapsed at the end of 2020 — check whether it has been renewed before claiming it.

levers.title: Claim the Pharmaceutical Appendix (K) on gels and placebo kits
levers.saves: 5% on 3006.70 gels or 3006.93.80 placebo/trial kits, from any column-1 country
levers.appliesTo: 3006.70.00.00 and 3006.93.80.00 (the dutiable lines that carry "K" in the Special column)
levers.document: Identification of the product by its INN (or a salt, ester or hydrate of one) listed in the Pharmaceutical Appendix.
levers.caveat: K applies only to products listed in the Pharmaceutical Appendix; a plain lubricant or a placebo with no listed ingredient will not qualify. Check the appendix before claiming.

levers.title: Get the line right — several Chapter 30 lines sit next to a free or out-of-scope alternative
levers.saves: Up to the full base rate (e.g. 5% on a gel, 6.4% on a starch placebo) and decides whether Section 232 reporting and the Section 301 exemption apply
levers.appliesTo: Gels (3006.70, 5%) vs. medicated gels in 3004 (Free); placebos packaged with medicinal preparations (3006.93.10, Free) vs. other placebos (3006.93.20–.80, dutiable); in-vivo diagnostic reagents (3006.30) vs. in-vitro reagents (3822); vitamin preparations (3004.50) vs. dietary supplements (2106.90, 6.4%); bulk hormones and vitamins (2936/2937) vs. medicaments (3003/3004)
levers.document: Product formulation, labeling and intended use; the Chapter 30 notes decide most of these splits.
levers.caveat: Classification follows what the product is, not the rate you want; a misclassification is a penalty exposure, not a saving. Get a ruling when in doubt.

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Duty on the middleman's markup — material when Section 232 (15–100%) or Section 301 (10–12.5%) applies
levers.appliesTo: Any line with an ad valorem duty: the six dutiable 3006 lines, the 77 Section 232 lines, and lines outside the Section 301 exemption
levers.document: The manufacturer-to-middleman invoice and proof it was a bona fide sale at arm's length, for goods clearly destined for the United States at that time.
levers.caveat: Related-party transfer prices must still pass the arm's-length tests; declare that you are using the earlier sale.

levers.title: Recover duties on goods you re-export or use to make exports
levers.saves: Up to 99% of duties paid — the proclamation expressly allows drawback of Section 232 pharma duties
levers.appliesTo: Any line where duty was paid, including Section 232 and Section 301 duties
levers.document: A drawback claim with import entries matched to export records (manufacturing, unused-merchandise or rejected-merchandise drawback).
levers.caveat: Claims must be filed within 5 years of import; substitution rules require goods of the same 8-digit classification.

levers.title: Hold or process goods in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: Cash flow (duty paid only when goods leave the zone for the U.S. market) and no duty on goods re-exported or destroyed in the zone
levers.document: FTZ admission (CBP Form 214) and zone inventory records.
levers.caveat: Section 232 pharma goods must be admitted in privileged foreign status, so a zone cannot be used to swap a 100% rate for a lower rate on the finished product.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the purpose fits
levers.saves: The base rate: each provision below is Free. Chapter 98 entries are also outside the Section 301 forced-labor duties
levers.appliesTo: Goods imported for a specific purpose, whatever their Chapter 30 line
levers.document: Evidence of the qualifying purpose: export records for returned goods; a bond and export/destruction proof for 9813.00.30.
levers.caveat: Section 232 duties still apply to Chapter 98 entries of covered pharmaceuticals (U.S. note 40(b)) — use the non-commercial heading 9903.04.70 or the U.S.-origin exemption where it fits. Goods under bond must be exported or destroyed under CBP supervision within the bond period.

provisions.text: U.S.-made Chapter 30 goods returned without being advanced in value abroad (e.g. returned or recalled product)
Articles solely for testing, experimental or review purposes
Samples valued at $1 or less each, or marked unfit for sale, used only to solicit orders

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification — and with it Section 232 scope and the Section 301 exemption — before goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate or the Chapter 99 treatment
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its composition and use.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; patent status and country of origin for Section 232 are facts CBP may still verify at entry.

rules.title: Every entry is transmitted to FDA through ACE; FDA can examine, detain and refuse goods that appear adulterated, misbranded or unapproved
Drugs: the foreign maker must be registered with FDA, name a U.S. agent, and list the product (NDC); the registration and listing numbers go on the entry
Drugs: an approved NDA/ANDA that names the foreign site (or, for OTC drugs, conformity with an OTC monograph); unapproved new drugs are refused
Investigational drugs, placebos and clinical-trial kits: import under an IND, consigned to the sponsor or investigator
Animal drugs: an approved (or conditionally approved / indexed) animal drug application, with the application number on the entry
Biologics (blood products, antisera, antibodies, vaccines, toxins): a biologics license and its number on the entry; some lots need FDA release
Human cells and tissues (HCT/Ps): import rules for cell-based products, held until FDA admits them
Prescription drugs in finished form: DSCSA product identifier on each package and transaction data passed to the next owner (the importer is a trading partner)

Controlled substances (opioids, benzodiazepines, anabolic steroids, etc.): DEA importer registration plus an import permit (Schedules I–II, narcotics in III–V) or import declaration (non-narcotics in III–V) for each shipment
Ephedrine, pseudoephedrine and norephedrine (List I chemicals, including drug products containing them): DEA Form 486 import notice at least 15 days ahead
Section 232 pharmaceuticals: the entry must report one Chapter 99 heading from 9903.04.60–9903.04.70, even when no extra duty is due

citations.label: HTSUS ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 40

rules.title: Veterinary vaccines and other veterinary biologics: a USDA permit to import (not FDA)
Animal-origin material (glands, organs, serum such as fetal bovine serum, animal cell cultures, organisms): VS import permit and origin certification; BSE restrictions on ruminant glands and serum
Infectious biological agents and materials that may contain them: CDC import permit

rules.agency: CDC Federal Select Agent Program / Commerce BIS
rules.title: Ricin: a regulated select-agent toxin and a Chemical Weapons Convention Schedule 1 chemical — registration and advance import notification
Material from wild animals: Form 3-177 at entry, and CITES permits for listed species

Medical devices (dressings, sutures, dental cements, lubricant gels, ostomy appliances): foreign establishment registration and listing, a U.S. agent, 510(k) clearance where the device class requires it
Waste pharmaceuticals that are hazardous waste: import only with EPA consent and a manifest
Individuals: personal importation is enforcement discretion, not a right — generally up to a 90-day supply for personal use; not a route for commercial goods

groups.label: Glands, organ extracts & heparin
groups.note: Animal-derived material (porcine heparin, bovine glands) needs USDA clearance as well as FDA; material from wild species also goes through Fish & Wildlife. None of the 3001 lines is in the Section 232 list.

groups.label: Blood, antisera, vaccines, toxins & cell cultures
groups.note: Split by product: human biologics clear FDA under a license; veterinary vaccines (3002.42) clear USDA, not FDA; fetal bovine serum needs a USDA permit; ricin is a select-agent toxin. 15 of the heading's 10-digit lines carry Section 232 reporting.

groups.label: Medicaments in bulk (not in doses)
groups.note: Bulk medicaments are usually inputs for U.S. finishing: the foreign plant must be registered and named in the U.S. application. Scheduled drugs need DEA permits; ephedrine-family products need a DEA import notice. 9 lines are in the Section 232 list.

groups.label: Medicaments in doses or retail packs
groups.note: The bulk of the chapter's value. Prescription drugs also fall under DSCSA tracing; "For veterinary use" lines go through FDA's animal-drug rules; scheduled drugs need DEA permits. 53 lines are in the Section 232 list. FDA prior notice does not apply — it is a food rule.

groups.label: Wadding, gauze, bandages & dressings
groups.note: Most dressings are FDA devices (some medicated dressings are combination products). These lines are outside the Section 301 pharmaceutical exemption.

groups.label: Other pharmaceutical goods (sutures, contrast, kits, ostomy, placebos)
groups.note: Mixed: sutures, dental cements, first-aid kits, gels and ostomy appliances are devices; contrast agents and contraceptives are drugs; clinical-trial kits enter under an IND; waste pharmaceuticals are an EPA matter. All six dutiable lines in the chapter are here.

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 30: Pharmaceutical Products — Tariff FAQ

seo.title: Pharmaceutical Tariffs FAQ: Ireland, India, Canada, China, Generic Drugs, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 30) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people actually search about pharmaceutical tariffs: the 100% Section 232 duty, generic drugs, medicine from India, Canada, China and the EU, and HS codes for medicines and vaccines.
keywords: can you import medicine into the us
does the us get medicine from china
hs code for vaccines for human medicine
importation of drugs into the united states

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing pharmaceuticals into the U.S. — tariffs by country, the Section 232 duty, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Almost every Chapter 30 line has a Free base rate; the cost comes from the Section 232 duty on patented drugs.
Patented drugs on the Section 232 list pay 100%, or 15% from the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland and 0% from the UK. Generics pay nothing extra.
FDA approval, registration and listing decide whether a drug can be imported at all — check them before the tariff.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on pharmaceuticals from Ireland?
searchedAs: us tariffs on pharmaceuticals from eu
faqs.answer: Yes, on patented drugs. Ireland is in the EU, so patented medicines on the Section 232 list pay 15% of their value in place of the base rate (9903.04.62). Generic drugs pay nothing extra, and the base rate on almost every Chapter 30 line is Free. Ireland supplied $42.6B of the $213.8B the U.S. imported in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on medicine from India?
searchedAs: tariffs on generic drugs from india
us tariff on medicine from india
faqs.answer: Generic medicines, most of what India ships, pay nothing: the base rate is Free and generics are excluded from the Section 232 duty (9903.04.67) and from the Section 301 tariffs. Patented drugs on the Section 232 list pay 100%, because India has no reduced rate. Bandages and a few other 3006 lines pay an extra 10% under Section 301.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on medicine from Canada?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on medicine from canada
is there a tariff on prescription drugs from canada
faqs.answer: Most medicines from Canada enter Free. Canada has no reduced Section 232 rate, so patented drugs on the Section 232 list pay 100% unless the maker has a company agreement; USMCA does not remove a Section 232 duty. USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the Section 301 tariffs. Personal imports of prescription drugs are an FDA question, not a tariff one.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on pharmaceuticals and medical supplies from China?
searchedAs: tariffs on medical supplies from china
does the us get medicine from china
faqs.answer: Generic medicines pay nothing extra. Patented drugs on the Section 232 list pay 100%. Bandages, dressings and a few 3006 lines pay 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action, and some 3006.93 placebo and clinical-trial products still carry the older China Section 301 duties (+25% or +7.5%). China supplied $5.4B of Chapter 30 goods in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on generic drugs?
faqs.answer: No. Generic drugs and biosimilars are excluded from the Section 232 pharmaceutical duty (9903.04.67), almost all Chapter 30 lines have a Free base rate, and medicines are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs. The 100% rate applies only to patented drugs on the Section 232 list.

faqs.question: What is the 100% pharmaceutical tariff, and when did it start?
faqs.answer: It is the Section 232 duty on patented pharmaceuticals (Proclamation 11020, April 2, 2026). It started on July 31, 2026 for 17 large drugmakers and on September 29, 2026 for everyone else. The 100% rate is the default; the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland pay 15%, the UK 0%, and companies with onshoring and pricing agreements 0%. The September 2025 announcement of 100% from October 1, 2025 was never put into effect.

faqs.question: Which drugs are on the pharmaceutical tariff list?
faqs.answer: The Section 232 list covers 77 Chapter 30 tariff lines in headings 3002, 3003 and 3004 — antibodies and other immunological products, insulin, hormones and most dosed medicines. Nothing in 3001, 3005 or 3006 is on it. Being on a listed line is not enough: the duty applies only to patented products, so generics on the same lines pay nothing.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for medicine?
faqs.answer: Medicines packed in doses or for retail sale — tablets, capsules, injections — are heading 3004; the same products in bulk are 3003. Vaccines, antibodies and blood products are 3002, bandages and dressings 3005. The overview has every 10-digit line, searchable by product name.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for vaccines?
searchedAs: hs code for vaccines for human medicine
faqs.answer: Vaccines for human medicine are 3002.41 and veterinary vaccines are 3002.42. Both have a Free base rate. Veterinary vaccines also need a USDA APHIS Center for Veterinary Biologics permit to be imported.

faqs.question: Can you import medicine into the U.S.?
searchedAs: can you import medicine into the us
importation of drugs into the united states
faqs.answer: Commercial imports must come from an FDA-registered establishment, be listed with FDA and covered by an approved application (NDA, ANDA or BLA) unless an exception applies; FDA reviews every drug entry. Controlled substances also need DEA import permits or declarations. Individuals can bring small personal supplies only under FDA's personal-importation policy.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on pharmaceuticals from the EU?
searchedAs: us tariffs on pharmaceuticals from eu
faqs.answer: Patented drugs on the Section 232 list pay 15% of value in place of the base rate (9903.04.62), the rate agreed in the EU–U.S. framework. Generics pay nothing extra. Bandages, dressings and four 3006 subheadings pay 10% in place of the base rate under Section 301. The EU — mainly Ireland, Germany, Belgium, France, Italy and the Netherlands — supplied over half of 2025 imports.
